title: Can the UK drive middle power coordination on AI?
gist: Chatham House argues the UK should sign the 20-country-plus-EU middle-power statement on frontier AI control and use its 2027 G20 presidency to build diplomatic infrastructure, possibly an FSB-style Technology Stability Board, for AI risk monitoring and incident reporting.

insights.claim: A group of 20 countries and the EU led by Norway and Finland, including Australia, Canada, Singapore and the UAE, issued a joint statement calling for measures to control frontier AI models, and the UK did not sign.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Middle powers are forming an AI-governance bloc distinct from US and China positions.

insights.claim: The US and China dominate up to 90% of compute, so middle powers cannot compete on AI capex and must choose between aligning, hedging, specializing in supply chain footholds, or coordinating.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Compute concentration frames why sovereign-AI strategies depend on coordination.
insights.locator: The US and China dominate up to 90 per cent of compute

insights.claim: Chatham House argues middle-power status is itself forged through coordination, citing Cohere and Aleph Alpha forming a 'transatlantic sovereign AI solution' and Canada and Germany committing £300M to a non-profit AI safety start-up.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Cross-border sovereign AI tie-ups are an emerging structure to watch among non-US labs.

insights.claim: Canada has called for a Technology Stability Board modelled on the post-crash Financial Stability Board, and the UK could use its G20 presidency to design such an arrangement enabling mandatory testing and serious-incident information sharing.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: An FSB-style AI body would be a new global regulatory layer affecting frontier labs.
insights.locator: Using the G20 to design an FSB-style arrangement

insights.claim: Middle powers worry their access to American proprietary models such as Claude or GPT-5 is not guaranteed, and some fear dependence on Chinese open-weight models.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Access risk to frontier models drives demand for sovereign and domestic alternatives.
insights.locator: Many realize their access to mostly American proprietary models

insights.claim: The UK's AI Security Institute reportedly faces the risk that US companies may be pressured by the White House not to send models for immediate testing, and summer U-turns over non-US access to Anthropic's latest models illustrate US volatility as a partner.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: US export-style control over frontier model access is a policy risk for non-US users and evaluators.

insights.claim: Washington could retaliate against middle powers regulating AI safety in ways it sees as unfriendly, while China's World AI Cooperation Organization offers an alternative that may tempt some middle powers.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Middle-power AI bloc building will be shaped by US retaliation risk and Chinese counter-offers.

insights.claim: The UK should sign the middle-power statement and use 2027 summits, including the G20 Geneva AI Summit and UN Global Dialogue, to broker agreement on risk monitoring, independent evaluations and incident reporting.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The UK's G20 presidency makes it a possible convener of a multilateral AI-security agreement.
insights.locator: The UK should sign the middle powers’ statement on AI security

insights.claim: UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan announced measures to boost resilience to AI-driven risks, including cyber defence and considering legislation to mandate serious AI incident reporting.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Mandatory AI incident reporting in the UK would add compliance obligations for model providers.
insights.locator: Last week, UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan announced
